prompt: What does an energy above the convex hull (E_hull) equal to 0 eV/atom indicate in a materials database?

options.text: The phase is predicted to be thermodynamically stable against competing phases in that database at 0 K
options.why: On-hull phases have E_hull = 0 relative to the competing entries in the same functional set.

options.text: The material has a zero band gap and must be a metal
options.why: E_hull measures thermodynamic stability, not electronic band gap.

options.text: The calculation failed to converge
options.why: E_hull = 0 means the entry sits on the lower convex hull.

hints: Distinguish thermodynamic phase stability from electronic band structure.
On the hull means no mixture of other phases in the database is lower in energy.

visual.none: The question is about the meaning of a database field; no plot on this site draws a convex hull.

prompt: Why should you treat band gaps listed in a high-throughput GGA/GGA+U database with caution?

options.text: Semi-local GGA functionals systematically underestimate semiconductor and insulator band gaps
options.why: Derivative discontinuity errors in semi-local DFT lead to underestimated gaps.

options.text: Databases only store optical absorption coefficients, not band gaps
options.why: Materials Project stores Kohn-Sham band gaps, which reflect the chosen functional.

options.text: GGA always overestimates band gaps by a factor of three
options.why: Semi-local GGA underestimates rather than overestimates band gaps.

hints: Recall the functional ladder and the band-gap problem from module 5.

prompt: Why is filtering by site count (nsites) useful before launching a first VASP project from a screening shortlist?

options.text: Plane-wave DFT scales steeply with atom count and volume, so smaller cells give faster starter runs
options.why: Keeping starter cells compact makes convergence testing and debugging practical.

options.text: VASP rejects any POSCAR with more than 10 atoms
options.why: VASP supports large supercells, but compute cost grows rapidly with atom count.

options.text: Larger cells never require k-points
options.why: k-mesh density depends on reciprocal lattice lengths, not just atom count.

hints: Think about how the cost of a plane-wave run grows with the number of atoms.

prompt: What does the live validity panel in the Material Builder check before you export a POSCAR?

options.text: Geometric and chemical issues such as overlapping atoms, short contacts, degenerate cells, duplicate atoms and charge neutrality
options.why: Rules B001 to B012 cover overlaps against covalent radii, short contacts, impossible packing, nearly degenerate cells, charge neutrality, Pauling rules, a perovskite check, periodic images and symmetry, all before export.

options.text: Whether your HPC cluster queue is currently empty
options.why: The Material Builder runs offline in the browser with no cluster connection.

options.text: The exact experimental melting point of the crystal
options.why: Validity rules check structure geometry and chemistry, not melting points.

prompt: Which ISIF setting should you use in VASP when relaxing a slab or a molecule placed in a vacuum box?

options.text: ISIF = 2 (relax atomic positions while keeping cell shape and volume fixed)
options.why: ISIF = 3 would collapse the vacuum gap.

options.text: ISIF = 3 (relax cell volume and shape freely)
options.why: ISIF = 3 shrinks the vacuum region around a slab or molecule.

options.text: ISIF = 7 (change volume only)
options.why: Volume relaxation collapses the vacuum gap.

hints: Think about what happens to empty vacuum space if VASP optimizes the cell volume.
Which ISIF value relaxes positions only?

prompt: How does the Material Builder detect severely overlapping atoms in a periodic crystal?

options.text: By comparing periodic minimum-image pair distances against Cordero covalent radii
options.why: Periodic minimum-image checks catch overlaps both inside the cell and across cell boundaries.

options.text: By running a full VASP SCF calculation in the browser
options.why: The overlap check is a fast geometric distance check.

options.text: By checking only the file size in bytes
options.why: File size says nothing about interatomic distances.

hints: Which radii does the Builder compare distances with?
Do periodic images count as neighbours?

prompt: What is the purpose of Molecule mode's 'Clean up in 3D' button?

options.text: It generates a rough starting 3D geometry for DFT using a valence-geometry heuristic, not a final quantum-chemical optimization
options.why: The 3D clean-up gives a reasonable starting POSCAR/XYZ that still needs DFT relaxation.

options.text: It runs CCSD(T) in the browser to compute exact bond lengths
options.why: It uses a lightweight local valence-geometry heuristic labelled with a Heuristic badge.

options.text: It deletes all hydrogen atoms before export
options.why: It expands explicit hydrogens so every atom has 3D coordinates.

prompt: For the 3.905 Å cubic perovskite template, "Defect supercell (>= 10 A)" builds a cell of 16 copies (80 atoms) instead of the 3×3×3 cell (135 atoms). Why?

options.text: It searches all supercells up to 64 copies for the fewest atoms whose shortest lattice vector is at least 10 Å, and a non-diagonal cell of 16 copies already reaches about 11 Å
options.why: A non-diagonal matrix with determinant 16 gives vectors of at least 2 sqrt(2) a, about 11 Å, with far fewer atoms than the diagonal 3×3×3 cell.

options.text: It always doubles the cell four times
options.why: The search picks the smallest determinant that meets the distance; for another cell it can be a different number.

options.text: VASP cannot run cells with more than 100 atoms
options.why: VASP runs much larger cells; the choice is about cost for a given image distance.

hints: How many atoms does a cell of det(M) copies hold?
Is the shortest lattice vector of a non-diagonal supercell always a multiple of a?

prompt: The equation-of-state fit warns that its minimum lies outside the sampled volumes. What should you do?

options.text: Run more volumes on the other side of the minimum so the points bracket it, then fit again
options.why: A fit that extrapolates past the data gives an unreliable V0 and an especially unreliable B0 prime.

options.text: Switch from Birch-Murnaghan to Murnaghan to remove the warning
options.why: Changing the form does not add data; the extrapolation problem stays.

options.text: Ignore it, since the bulk modulus does not depend on the minimum
options.why: B0 is the curvature at the minimum, so it depends on where the minimum is.

hints: What does extrapolation do to a fitted curvature?
B0 is defined at V0.

prompt: A result on the site carries the badge "Heuristic". How should you use it?

options.text: As a rule of thumb to decide what to run, not as a result to report
options.why: Tolerance factors, feasibility verdicts and cost estimates are useful guides, but they are not computed properties of the material.

options.text: As an exact value computed from your files
options.why: That is the "computed" badge; a heuristic rests on an empirical rule.

options.text: As a toy model that has nothing to do with real materials
options.why: Toy models carry their own badge; heuristics do apply to real materials, only approximately.

prompt: For the cubic LaCuO3 cell with a = 3.88 Å and KSPACING = 0.2 per Å, how many k-points does VASP use along each axis?

options.why: N = ceil(|b| / KSPACING) with |b| = 2 pi / a = 1.619 per Å, so 1.619 / 0.2 = 8.1, rounded up to 9.
The formula rounds up, not to the nearest integer, so 8.1 becomes 9.
That forgets the factor 2 pi in the length of the reciprocal vector.

prompt: For one neutral oxygen vacancy in LaCuO3, which expression is the formation energy?

options.text: E_f = E_defect - E_bulk + mu_O
options.why: One O atom is removed, so n_O = -1 in E_f = E_defect - E_bulk - sum n_i mu_i, which turns the minus into a plus.

options.text: E_f = E_defect - E_bulk - mu_O
options.why: That would be the sign for an added O atom (an interstitial), not a removed one.

options.text: E_f = E_defect - E_bulk
options.why: The removed atom goes to a reservoir with chemical potential mu_O, which must be counted.

hints: Is n_O positive or negative for a vacancy?
Where does the removed atom go?

prompt: You run NdCuO3 with the Nd_3 POTCAR. What should MAGMOM hold for Nd?

options.text: Zero, because Nd_3 keeps the 4f electrons in the core, so there is no f moment to start
options.why: With the f shell frozen in the core the valence has no open f shell; a moment on Nd has nothing to act on.

options.text: 3 per Nd, one for each unpaired 4f electron of Nd3+
options.why: That would need the 4f electrons in the valence, which Nd_3 does not have.

options.text: The same value as Cu, so that all cations are treated alike
options.why: MAGMOM should reflect the expected moment of each species, and Cu and Nd differ.

hints: What does the _3 in the potential name stand for?
Where are the 4f electrons in this potential?

prompt: In the surface energy gamma = (E_slab - N E_bulk) / (2A) of a symmetric slab, why is there a factor 2?

options.text: The slab has two surfaces, top and bottom, both of area A
options.why: The excess energy of the slab over bulk is shared by two equal surfaces, so it is divided by twice the area.

options.text: To convert from eV to joules
options.why: Unit conversion uses the electron charge and the area unit, not a factor 2.

options.text: Because of spin polarization
options.why: The factor counts surfaces; spin does not enter the formula.

hints: How many surfaces does a slab in a periodic cell with vacuum have?
What does symmetric mean here?

prompt: You move from single runs to a Python pipeline. Which habit keeps the results trustworthy?

options.text: Check representative runs by hand (moments, NELM, forces) and have the scripts test the same things in OSZICAR and OUTCAR
options.why: A run can finish normally after hitting NELM or losing its moments; the checks you made by hand must become part of the pipeline.

options.text: Trust the exit code: a run that exits normally is correct
options.why: VASP often exits normally from runs whose results are unusable.

options.text: Automate first and debug later on the full set
options.why: A mistake in the first run is then repeated in every run.

hints: What can a normal exit hide?
Which checks did Calculation Review make for you?

prompt: The Project Card estimates relative cost as (nsites / 4)^3, times 2 if spin-polarized. What does it give for a magnetic cell of 20 sites?

options.text: About 250 times a four-atom non-magnetic cell
options.why: (20 / 4)^3 = 125, and the factor 2 for two spin channels gives 250, at the same settings.

options.text: About 125 times
options.why: That leaves out the factor 2 for a spin-polarized run.

options.text: About 10 times
options.why: That treats the cost as linear in the atom count, but the large-cell scaling of plane-wave DFT is cubic.

hints: Compute (20 / 4)^3 first.
A spin-polarized run solves two spin channels.
